passRule: Pass = overall 70+ and no critical error. Hints cost 2 points each.
sbarRubric: Situation: who you are, who the patient is, the concern
Assessment: vital signs and what you think

cases.opening: My chest has been hurting for about 30 minutes. I feel short of breath and a little dizzy.

answers.onset: About half an hour ago, carrying shopping up the stairs.
answers.character: Heavy — like a weight crushing my chest.
answers.radiation: It goes into my left arm and my jaw.
answers.associated: I feel sick and sweaty, a bit short of breath, and dizzy.
answers.social: I smoke about fifteen a day. A few beers at the weekend.
answers.family: My dad had a heart attack at sixty.
answers.pain: It's in the middle of my chest, heavy, eight out of ten.

exams.general: Pale, sweaty, clutching his chest, anxious.
exams.airway: Talking in full sentences — airway clear.
exams.chest: Clear breath sounds both sides; no added sounds.
exams.circulation: Cool hands, capillary refill 3 seconds, regular radial pulse.

ecg.result: Sinus tachycardia 104/min with ST elevation in II, III and aVF — inferior STEMI.

cxr.result: Normal heart size; clear lungs; no widened mediastinum.

actions.label: Let him walk to the bathroom
actions.harm: A patient with suspected heart attack stays on bed rest and on a monitor; exertion can extend the damage or trigger a dangerous arrhythmia.

effect.line: Thank you. It still hurts but I feel safer.
It's getting worse… I feel faint.

deterioration.warning: He is greyer and sweatier; the pain is worse.
He is drowsy and clammy — possible cardiogenic shock.

diagnosis.label: Pulmonary embolism
diagnosis.why: PE causes breathlessness and tachycardia, but not ST elevation in II, III and aVF.

diagnosis.label: Aortic dissection
diagnosis.why: Worth excluding (tearing pain to the back, unequal pulses), but the ECG points to STEMI.

diagnosis.label: Reflux
diagnosis.why: Dangerous causes must be excluded first.

nursingPriority.label: Reduced cardiac perfusion — ECG, monitoring and immediate escalation
Anxiety — reassure and wait
nursingPriority.why: Anxiety is real but secondary; chest pain needs an ECG first.

cases.goodOutcome: Mr Hayes had an inferior STEMI. The fast ECG and escalation got him to the cath lab, where his blocked right coronary artery was opened. He went home on day 4.
cases.badOutcome: The ECG or escalation was delayed. Mr Hayes developed cardiogenic shock before his artery was opened; he survived but with more heart muscle damage.
teaching: ECG within 10 minutes of arrival for chest pain
STEMI is a time-critical emergency: escalate immediately
Check allergies before every medicine

cases.opening: I… can't get… my breath… my inhaler… isn't working.

answers.onset: Since… last night… worse… this morning.
answers.meds: Blue inhaler… ten puffs… no help.
answers.history: Asthma… one admission… two years ago.

exams.general: Sitting forward, using neck muscles to breathe, speaking in short phrases.
exams.chest: Widespread expiratory wheeze; reduced air entry at both bases.

abg.result: pH 7.45, low CO₂, low O₂ — hyperventilating, not yet tiring.

actions.label: Lie her flat
actions.harm: Lying flat makes breathing harder for a breathless patient. Keep her sitting up.

effect.line: That's… helping. I can breathe a bit better.

actions.label: Give a sedative to calm her
actions.harm: Sedatives suppress breathing in acute asthma and can cause respiratory arrest.

deterioration.warning: She can only speak single words now.
She is becoming drowsy — a sign of life-threatening asthma.

diagnosis.label: Anaphylaxis
diagnosis.why: Reasonable to consider with wheeze, but there is no trigger, rash or swelling.

diagnosis.label: Pneumothorax
diagnosis.why: Air entry is reduced on both sides with wheeze, which fits asthma.

diagnosis.label: Panic attack
diagnosis.why: Low oxygen saturation and wheeze are objective signs of disease.

nursingPriority.label: Impaired gas exchange — oxygen, bronchodilator, close monitoring
Anxiety
nursingPriority.why: She is anxious because she cannot breathe.

nursingPriority.label: Inhaler technique teaching
nursingPriority.why: Important later, once she is stable.

cases.goodOutcome: With oxygen and nebulisers early, Ms Torres's breathing settled within an hour. She went home the next day with a written asthma plan.
cases.badOutcome: Treatment came late; she tired and needed ICU review for breathing support.
teaching: Severe asthma: oxygen to 94–98% and bronchodilators immediately
Drowsiness and a "silent chest" are life-threatening signs
Never sedate an acutely breathless patient

cases.opening: Where… where am I? I feel so cold.

answers.pain: My chest hurts when I cough.

exams.general: Flushed, shivering, confused about place and time.
exams.chest: Coarse crackles and bronchial breathing at the right base.
exams.circulation: Mottled knees; capillary refill 4 seconds; urine output 10 mL last hour.
exams.neuro: New confusion (was orientated yesterday); pupils equal.

cultures.result: Two sets taken; results in 24–48 hours.

effect.line: I feel a little less dizzy.

actions.label: Give the prescribed piperacillin-tazobactam
actions.harm: Piperacillin-tazobactam is a penicillin and his chart records a penicillin allergy. Stop and ask the prescriber for an alternative.

actions.label: Give the re-prescribed non-penicillin IV antibiotic

deterioration.warning: He is more mottled and barely passing urine.
He is more confused; temperature rising.

diagnosis.label: Septic shock from right lower lobe pneumonia
Cardiogenic shock
diagnosis.why: Warm, flushed, fever and consolidation point to infection.

diagnosis.label: Dehydration
diagnosis.why: He is dry, but fever, high white cells and lactate mean sepsis.

diagnosis.label: COPD exacerbation only
diagnosis.why: Does not explain the shock.

nursingPriority.label: Ineffective tissue perfusion — sepsis: escalate, fluids, cultures, antibiotics
Acute confusion — reorientation
nursingPriority.why: His confusion is caused by poor perfusion; treat the cause.

nursingPriority.label: Fever — cooling only
nursingPriority.why: Treating the number misses the sepsis.

cases.goodOutcome: Early fluids, cultures and a safe antibiotic turned Mr Kim around; his lactate fell and he left ICU on day 3.
cases.badOutcome: Delays in fluids or antibiotics let his shock worsen; he needed vasopressors and a longer ICU stay.
teaching: Sepsis: cultures, lactate, fluids and antibiotics within the first hour
Always check the allergy record against the prescription
COPD: target saturation 88–92%

cases.opening: Morning. It really hurts around my tummy when I move.

answers.severity: About a seven out of ten, worse when I cough.
answers.pain: Around the cuts and my right shoulder. About seven out of ten.
answers.onset: Since I woke up from the anaesthetic, worse this morning.
answers.associated: A bit sick last night. No vomiting today.
answers.last_meal: Just sips of water so far.

exams.general: Lying very still, guarding her abdomen.
exams.wound: Four port sites clean and dry; no bleeding or redness.
exams.chest: Reduced air entry at the bases — shallow breathing.

effect.line: Oh, that's much better, thank you.

actions.label: Give codeine
actions.harm: She is allergic to codeine (vomiting). Never give a medicine listed on the allergy record.

actions.label: Help her sit out in the chair

effect.line: It's really bad when I breathe in.

deterioration.warning: She is breathing shallowly because of pain — risk of a chest infection.

diagnosis.label: Bile leak
diagnosis.why: Worth watching for (fever, rising pain, jaundice), but her abdomen is soft.

diagnosis.label: DVT
diagnosis.why: Calves are soft and non-tender.

nursingPriority.label: Acute pain — assess, treat with prescribed analgesia, reassess
Wound infection risk
nursingPriority.why: Monitor, but the wounds are clean.

cases.goodOutcome: With her pain controlled Ms Park breathed deeply, walked by the afternoon and went home the next day.
cases.badOutcome: Uncontrolled pain kept her breathing shallow; she developed a low-grade fever from a chest infection and stayed two extra days.
teaching: Assess, treat and reassess pain
Check the allergy record before every medicine
Post-op: deep breathing and early mobilisation prevent complications

cases.complaint: Unsteady on his feet after a fall at home
cases.opening: Hello, dear. Is it morning already? I need the toilet.

answers.fall: I fell in the kitchen last week. My legs go wobbly when I stand up.
answers.toilet: I need to go quite a lot at night — those water tablets.
answers.social: I live alone since my wife passed. My daughter visits on Sundays.

exams.mobility: Unsteady; shuffling gait; needs a walking frame and one person.
exams.skin: Redness over the sacrum that blanches — early pressure risk.
exams.general: Pleasant, slightly muddled about the day.
exams.neuro: Alert; orientated to person, not to day.

actions.label: Falls bundle: low bed, call bell in reach, non-slip socks, frame nearby
Walk him to the bathroom with his frame
Put all four bed rails up
actions.harm: Full rails on a confused patient can lead to climbing over them — a worse fall. Use a low bed and frequent checks.

actions.label: Restrain him to the bed
actions.harm: Restraint is not fall prevention; it causes injury and distress, and needs strict criteria and a physician order.

effect.line: I needed the toilet and nobody came.

deterioration.warning: He tried to get up alone to use the bathroom and nearly fell.

nursingPriority.label: Risk of falls — falls bundle, assisted toileting, postural BP
Risk of pressure injury
nursingPriority.why: Important too, but a fall is the bigger immediate risk.

cases.goodOutcome: Mr Jensen stayed safe overnight. The postural drop was reported, his diuretic timing was changed and physiotherapy planned his discharge.
cases.badOutcome: Without precautions he got up alone and fell, bruising his hip; an incident report was filed.
teaching: Assess falls risk on admission and after any change
Low bed and call bell, not restraint
Lying and standing BP when a patient feels dizzy on standing

cases.complaint: Diabetic, shaky and sweaty before breakfast
cases.arrival: Bed 2, admitted for a foot ulcer
cases.opening: I feel shaky and sweaty… I didn't eat much last night.

answers.last_meal: I only had a bit of soup last night. I wasn't hungry.
answers.associated: Shaky, sweaty, a bit of a headache.
answers.meds: My long insulin at night and the short one with meals.
answers.previous: It happened once at home. My husband gave me juice.

exams.general: Pale, sweaty, tremor in her hands.
exams.wound: Ulcer on the left heel, clean dressing, no spreading redness.

actions.label: Give her scheduled mealtime insulin now
actions.harm: Giving insulin to a hypoglycaemic patient drops her glucose further and can cause seizures or coma. Treat the low and recheck first.

actions.label: Give a longer-acting snack/meal once glucose is up
Teach hypoglycaemia signs and meal timing

deterioration.warning: She is confused and sweating — her glucose is falling.

diagnosis.label: Sepsis from the foot ulcer
diagnosis.why: No fever; the ulcer looks clean; the glucose explains it.

diagnosis.label: Anxiety
diagnosis.why: Measure the glucose first.

nursingPriority.label: Unstable blood glucose — treat, recheck, inform, educate
Impaired skin integrity (ulcer)
nursingPriority.why: Ongoing, but the low glucose is urgent.

cases.goodOutcome: Her glucose recovered quickly, the physician reduced her mealtime insulin and she had no further lows.
cases.badOutcome: The low glucose was missed; she became confused and needed IV glucose.
teaching: Check glucose in any unwell diabetic patient
Treat a low with fast-acting glucose, recheck in 15 minutes
Never give insulin to a hypoglycaemic patient

cases.opening: (His mother:) He's been coughing for three days and today he won't feed. He's breathing so fast.

answers.onset: (Mother:) A runny nose four days ago, then the cough.
answers.associated: (Mother:) He's feeding half as much. Fewer wet diapers — three today.
answers.family: (Mother:) His big sister has a cold.

exams.general: Tired baby, nasal flaring, head bobbing.
exams.chest: Fine crackles and wheeze on both sides; subcostal recession.
exams.hydration: Mouth slightly dry; fontanelle normal; 3 wet diapers today.

actions.label: Small, frequent feeds and a feeding chart
Explain the plan to his mother and involve her

deterioration.warning: More recession and head bobbing — he is working harder.

diagnosis.label: Bacterial pneumonia
diagnosis.why: Possible, but bilateral crackles and wheeze after a cold fit bronchiolitis.

diagnosis.label: Asthma
diagnosis.why: Asthma is not diagnosed at 7 months.

nursingPriority.label: Impaired gas exchange and poor feeding — oxygen, suction, feeds, escalate

cases.goodOutcome: Leo needed oxygen for two days and went home feeding well.
cases.badOutcome: Oxygen came late; he tired and needed high-flow support on the pediatric high-dependency unit.
teaching: Use pediatric ranges: a respiratory rate of 58 is fast for 7 months
Bronchiolitis is supportive care: oxygen, suction, feeds
Involve parents in the plan

cases.opening: I feel a lot of blood coming… and I'm a bit dizzy.

exams.fundus: Uterus soft and boggy, above the umbilicus; heavy fresh bleeding.

effect.line: The cramping is stronger… but I feel less dizzy.

actions.label: Weigh pads to estimate blood loss
Leave to fetch supplies
actions.harm: Never leave a bleeding patient alone. Use the emergency bell and call for help.

deterioration.warning: Bleeding heavier — pads soaked through; uterus boggy.
She is drowsy and grey — hemorrhagic shock.

diagnosis.label: Primary postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony
Genital tract tear
diagnosis.why: One of the "4 Ts" to check, but a boggy uterus points to tone.

diagnosis.label: Retained placenta
diagnosis.why: The placenta was complete.

nursingPriority.label: Risk of hemorrhagic shock — massage, call for help, IV access, protocol

cases.goodOutcome: Fundal massage and the protocol stopped the bleeding at an estimated 900 mL. Ms Rahman needed no transfusion and fed her baby that evening.
cases.badOutcome: Help and treatment were delayed; she lost over 2 litres and needed a transfusion and theatre.
teaching: PPH: the 4 Ts — tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin
Massage the uterus and call for help immediately
Quantify blood loss; never leave the patient alone

cases.complaint: Right knee arthroscopy — surgical safety checklist
cases.opening: Morning. I'm a bit nervous. Is it the right knee you're doing?

answers.site: My right knee. The surgeon saw me last week.
answers.allergies: Latex — I come out in hives.

exams.skin: There is no surgical site mark on the right knee.

actions.label: Call a stop: site not marked — surgeon to mark before proceeding
Proceed to theatre without the mark
actions.harm: Wrong-site surgery is a never event. The site must be marked and verified at the time-out before incision.

actions.label: Make the theatre latex-free and inform the team
Instrument and swab count (sign-in and sign-out)

requirements.label: Confirmed the site with the patient
Stopped the line until the site was marked

diagnosis.label: Not ready until the site is marked and the theatre is latex-free
Ready to proceed
diagnosis.why: The site was not marked.

nursingPriority.label: Surgical safety: identity, site, consent, allergy, count
Pre-op anxiety
nursingPriority.why: Reassure him, but the checklist comes first.

cases.goodOutcome: The time-out caught the missing site mark and the latex allergy. Surgery went ahead safely on the right knee.
cases.badOutcome: A checklist step was missed — a serious safety incident that was reported and investigated.
teaching: WHO surgical safety checklist: sign-in, time-out, sign-out
Anyone can stop the line
Allergies change the theatre set-up

cases.arrival: Bed 12; admitted 3 days ago with a chest infection, improving
cases.opening: Who are you? I need to get home to feed the cat.
history: Mild dementia? — no; daughter says she was sharp yesterday

answers.urine: It stings when I go… and I keep needing to go.
answers.onset: I don't know what you mean.

exams.neuro: Inattentive (cannot say months backwards); disorientated to place and time — positive delirium screen.
exams.hydration: Dry mouth; fluid chart shows 600 mL in 24 hours.
exams.chest: Few crackles at the left base, improving.

actions.label: Reorient calmly; glasses and hearing aid; call her daughter

effect.line: Oh… the hospital. Is Susan coming?

actions.label: Start a fluid balance chart and encourage drinks
Give a sedative for agitation
actions.harm: Sedating delirium hides the cause and raises the risk of falls and aspiration. Find and treat the cause.

deterioration.warning: She is trying to climb out of bed.

diagnosis.label: Delirium from urinary infection and dehydration
Dementia
diagnosis.why: Dementia is gradual; this is new since yesterday.

diagnosis.label: Stroke
diagnosis.why: Consider it, but there is no focal weakness and there is a clear infection.

nursingPriority.label: Acute confusion — find the cause, keep her safe, escalate
Risk of falls
nursingPriority.why: Yes, but treat the cause too.

cases.goodOutcome: The UTI and dehydration were treated; by day 2 Mrs Ellis was herself again.
cases.badOutcome: The confusion was not escalated; she fell trying to leave and her infection progressed.
teaching: New confusion is delirium until proven otherwise
Look for the cause: infection, dehydration, drugs, glucose, pain, constipation
Avoid sedation; reorient and involve family

cases.opening: My heart's been racing and fluttering since I woke up.

answers.onset: I woke up with it at six this morning. I was fine last night.
answers.associated: A bit breathless climbing stairs. No chest pain. No fainting.
answers.social: I have a few glasses of wine most nights.

exams.circulation: Irregularly irregular radial pulse; warm; capillary refill 2 seconds.

ecg.result: Atrial fibrillation with ventricular rate 148/min; no ST changes.

effect.line: The racing has settled a lot.

actions.label: Assess stroke and bleeding risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc, HAS-BLED)
Electrical cardioversion now
actions.harm: He is stable and the onset time is uncertain enough to need caution; cardioversion without anticoagulation risks a stroke. Rate control first.

diagnosis.label: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
SVT
diagnosis.why: Also fast, but SVT is regular; this is irregularly irregular.

diagnosis.label: Ventricular tachycardia
diagnosis.why: The QRS is narrow.

nursingPriority.label: Decreased cardiac output risk — monitor, ECG, escalate, give prescribed rate control

cases.goodOutcome: Rate control settled Mr Whitaker's heart rate; he started anticoagulation and went home with cardiology follow-up.
cases.badOutcome: Investigation was slow; his rate stayed fast and he spent longer in hospital.
teaching: Irregularly irregular pulse → ECG
Rate control, then think about stroke risk and anticoagulation
Onset time decides whether early cardioversion is safe

cases.complaint: Sudden right-sided weakness and slurred speech
cases.opening: My… arm… won't… work. (Her speech is slurred.)
history: Atrial fibrillation (stopped her blood thinner last month)

answers.lkw: (Daughter:) She was fine at 8:10 at breakfast. At 8:30 she couldn't lift her cup.
answers.meds: (Daughter:) Bisoprolol. She stopped her blood thinner last month — she didn't like it.

exams.fast: Right facial droop, right arm drifts down, slurred speech — FAST positive.
exams.neuro: Alert; right arm and leg weak (power 2/5); right visual field loss.
exams.general: Alert, frustrated, unable to find words.

ct_head.result: No hemorrhage. Early changes in the left middle cerebral artery territory.

actions.label: Keep nil by mouth until swallow screen
Give her morning tablets with water
actions.harm: She has not passed a swallow screen; with facial weakness she could aspirate. Keep her nil by mouth.

actions.label: Rapidly lower her blood pressure
actions.harm: In acute ischaemic stroke, rapid lowering can extend the brain injury; follow the stroke team's targets.

actions.label: Thrombolysis decision with the stroke team

deterioration.warning: Her speech is worse and the arm is now completely weak — time is brain.

diagnosis.label: Acute ischaemic stroke (left MCA), likely from AF
Intracerebral hemorrhage
diagnosis.why: Must be excluded by CT before any clot-busting drug.

diagnosis.label: Hypoglycaemia
diagnosis.why: Glucose is 112 mg/dL.

nursingPriority.label: Ineffective cerebral perfusion — stroke alert, glucose, nil by mouth, monitor neuro signs
Impaired mobility
nursingPriority.why: True, but acute treatment comes first.

cases.goodOutcome: The stroke alert, CT and last-known-well time allowed the stroke team to treat within the window. Ms Delgado regained much of her arm function.
cases.badOutcome: Delays used up the treatment window; she was left with significant weakness.
teaching: FAST, last-known-well time and glucose, then a stroke alert
CT excludes bleeding before thrombolysis
Nil by mouth until a swallow screen

cases.opening: I started shivering an hour ago. They told me to come in if I got a temperature.
history: Breast cancer; chemotherapy cycle 3 eight days ago

answers.onset: The shivering started about an hour ago.
answers.associated: Tired. A sore mouth. No cough, no burning when I pee.
answers.history: Breast cancer. Chemo every three weeks; the last was eight days ago.

cultures.result: Taken from the port and a vein.

actions.label: Give empirical IV antibiotics (neutropenic sepsis protocol)
Take a rectal temperature
actions.harm: Rectal measurements are avoided in neutropenic patients because of infection and bleeding risk.

actions.label: Give acetaminophen and recheck in an hour
actions.harm: Neutropenic fever is an emergency: antibiotics must start within an hour. Do not wait.

deterioration.warning: Rigors; blood pressure falling — neutropenic sepsis.

diagnosis.label: Viral illness
diagnosis.why: Never assume in a neutropenic patient.

diagnosis.label: Port infection
diagnosis.why: Possible source; cultures from the port help.

nursingPriority.label: Risk of sepsis — isolation, cultures, antibiotics within an hour, escalate

cases.goodOutcome: Antibiotics started within the hour; Ms Natarajan's fever settled and her counts recovered.
cases.badOutcome: Antibiotics were delayed; she developed septic shock and needed ICU.
teaching: Fever after chemotherapy = neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise
Antibiotics within 60 minutes; cultures first but never delay
No rectal temperatures in neutropenia

cases.complaint: Prescription check: amoxicillin for a chest infection
cases.opening: The doctor said I need antibiotics for this cough. Is that my medicine?

answers.allergies: Penicillin — my throat swelled up and I needed an EpiPen.

actions.label: Dispense the amoxicillin
actions.harm: Amoxicillin is a penicillin; he has had anaphylaxis to penicillin. Dispensing it could kill him.

actions.label: Suggest a non-penicillin alternative to the prescriber
Explain the change and allergy alert to the patient
Record the intervention and update the allergy alert

diagnosis.label: Prescription conflicts with a documented anaphylaxis — do not dispense
Safe to dispense
diagnosis.why: Amoxicillin is a penicillin.

nursingPriority.label: Medication safety — stop, contact prescriber, document

cases.goodOutcome: The prescriber changed the antibiotic; Mr Reed's allergy alert was updated on every system.
cases.badOutcome: A dangerous prescription was not stopped.
teaching: Check every prescription against the allergy record
Contact the prescriber with a safe alternative
Document interventions

cases.opening: I feel a bit weak, nurse. Is something wrong with my blood test?

answers.associated: Weak legs. A bit of tingling.
answers.meds: Spironolactone, lisinopril and my water tablet.

ecg.result: Sinus bradycardia 54/min with tall peaked T waves — hyperkalaemia changes.

actions.label: Phone the result to the responsible clinician and ask for a read-back
Give him a banana and orange juice
actions.harm: Both are high in potassium — this raises it further.

deterioration.warning: Heart rate falling; the monitor shows wide complexes.

diagnosis.label: Severe hyperkalaemia from CKD and medicines, with ECG changes
Hemolysed sample artefact
diagnosis.why: The sample was checked and the repeat confirms it.

nursingPriority.label: Risk of arrhythmia — ECG, monitor, escalate, follow protocol

cases.goodOutcome: The critical result was acted on within minutes; his potassium fell and the medicines were adjusted.
cases.badOutcome: Delays let his heart rate fall dangerously before treatment.
teaching: Critical results: verify, phone with read-back, document
Hyperkalaemia: ECG and monitor
Watch potassium-raising medicines in kidney disease

cases.complaint: CT abdomen with contrast — safety screening
cases.opening: Do I get the dye? Last time it made me itchy.

answers.allergies: The CT dye gave me hives two years ago.
answers.history: Diabetes and something with my kidneys.

actions.label: Inject contrast and scan
actions.harm: He has had a reaction to contrast and his kidney function is unknown. The radiologist must decide on premedication or an alternative first.

actions.label: Ask the radiologist to review the request
Advise on metformin per contrast policy

diagnosis.label: Contrast not safe as requested — previous reaction and low eGFR
Safe to proceed
diagnosis.why: Two red flags were present.

nursingPriority.label: Contrast safety — allergy, kidney function, metformin, radiologist review

cases.goodOutcome: The scan was changed to a safe alternative; Mr Alvarez had no reaction and no kidney injury.
cases.badOutcome: A safety check was skipped before contrast.
teaching: Screen for contrast allergy and kidney function before contrast
Metformin and contrast need a policy check
The radiologist decides when screening flags a risk

triage.name: Unknown man, about 30
triage.story: Found unresponsive by friends; pinpoint pupils; breathing slowly.
triage.why: Unresponsive with slow breathing — needs immediate resuscitation (level 1).

triage.name: Robert Hayes
triage.story: Crushing chest pain for 30 minutes, sweaty.
triage.why: High-risk chest pain — ECG within 10 minutes (level 2).

triage.name: Jasmine Lee
triage.story: 8 weeks pregnant, one-sided lower abdominal pain and light bleeding, dizzy.
triage.why: Possible ectopic pregnancy with signs of shock (level 2).

triage.name: Mia Chen
triage.story: Fever since yesterday; playful, drinking, wet diapers.
triage.why: Well-appearing child with fever, normal hydration (level 4).

triage.name: Carlos Ruiz
triage.story: Twisted ankle playing football; can bear weight with a limp.

triage.name: Ellen Brooks
triage.story: Small cut on the finger from a kitchen knife; bleeding stopped with pressure.
triage.why: Minor wound, no resources beyond a dressing (level 5).

shift.title: 7 AM shift — General Ward, bays 2–6
shift.brief: Night-shift handover: Bed 2 Grace Okoye — diabetic, did not eat much last night. Bed 4 Linda Park — day 1 after gallbladder surgery, asked for pain relief at 5 AM. Bed 6 Harold Jensen — 84, fell at home, needed the toilet several times overnight. Prioritise, care for each patient and give a handover at the end.
